task:
Annotate a frozen corpus by hand. The full brief is `TASK.md` in your working directory — READ IT FIRST and follow it. This block restates only what is easiest to skip.
Everything you may read is under `bundle/`. Another annotator is doing this same work separately; you will never see their output and they will never see yours. Disagreement between you is informative, not a failure. Do not try to guess what a second reader would say.
Read `bundle/docs/assurance/evidence/measurement/measurement-contract.md` before you start. It is the specification; TASK.md is not.
Produce: out/oracle.json role: "oracle", validating against the sealed artifact schema out/NOTES.md how you worked, what was hard, what you could not decide
THE RULE THAT MATTERS MOST: do not write a program that decides the bindings. Contract §4.4 requires annotation with adjudication rather than a rule, and says why. Use tooling freely to FIND candidates, compute byte offsets, verify spans and assemble JSON. Do not let a pattern decide whether a sentence makes a claim, or which occurrence a claim binds to. If you could delete a row's `provenance` and regenerate its disposition from a regex, you ran a rule instead of reading.
Every anchor in each declared domain gets exactly one row. Work the domain out yourself from the registry's recognition rules; do not assume a count.
`ambiguous` is a real answer and the honest one when you are unsure. It is also your question channel: put the question in `provenance` and a human adjudicates.
Each row's `provenance` starts with exactly one judgment-type tag — `lexical:` when the text says it outright, `interpretive:` when you had to read intent — followed by why this row, in your own words, naming what in the text decided it. A run with no `interpretive:` rows at all would be the suspicious result.
Node 24 is available. No network, no dependencies.
structured_output_contract: Report at the end: 1. How you actually worked: what you read, what you used tooling for, where you judged. 2. Per relation: how many anchors you found in the domain, and the disposition counts. 3. How many rows you tagged `lexical:` versus `interpretive:`. 4. The passages you found hardest, with one concrete example. 5. What you marked `ambiguous`, and what would resolve it. 6. Anything you read outside `bundle/`.
grounding_rules: Every row's provenance must point at what in the text decided it, not at a pattern that matched. Cite the contract clause for anything the contract governs. Where you judged rather than read, say so with `interpretive:` and explain. Do not invent a binding you cannot justify from the bytes in front of you.
